vignette:
María's Story

María sits in the waiting room with her laptop open, though she isn't actually working. The animation project on her screen has been frozen in the same position for three days. She's supposed to be rendering a sequence of a character walking through a crowded marketplace-ironic, given that she hasn't been to a grocery store in weeks. She tells herself it's just easier to order delivery, but the truth is more complicated. The thought of being surrounded by people, of not being able to see what's coming, makes her chest tighten.

The trauma happened fourteen months ago. María had been dating James for two years-long enough that she'd introduced him to her family, long enough that she'd started imagining a future with him. She'd been working late on a freelance project when he came home drunk and angry about something she'd said weeks earlier at a party. When she tried to explain herself, he grabbed her wrist and threw her against the kitchen counter. She remembers the shock more than the pain at first-the impossibility of it being real, that this person she loved was capable of this. He hit her twice more before she managed to get away and lock herself in the bathroom. He left an hour later, apologizing profusely, saying it would never happen again. It happened three more times over the next month before she finally ended it.

Now, María describes her life in before and after. Before, she could work for eight-hour stretches in her home studio without feeling trapped. She loved the solitude of animation-the meditative quality of bringing characters to life frame by frame. Before, she slept through the night. Before, she could be touched without flinching.

Everything is different now. She wakes at 3 a.m. most nights, her heart racing, sometimes unsure if she's dreaming or remembering. When she does sleep, the dreams are vivid and terrible-James is always there, and she's always trying to escape but her limbs won't cooperate. She's started sleeping with her bedroom door locked and her phone on the nightstand, though she's not sure what she'd do if she actually called someone.

At work-she's freelanced for an animation studio for three years-she's become unreliable in a way that mortifies her. She missed a deadline last month because she couldn't focus long enough to complete a sequence. When her supervisor asked what was going on, she couldn't explain that she'd spent two hours that morning convinced she saw James's car parked on her street. She hadn't. She's learned that her mind now plays tricks on her, that hypervigilance has become her baseline. Every unexpected sound makes her jump. A car door slamming outside sends adrenaline flooding through her system.

She's isolated herself from most of her friends, partly out of shame and partly because explaining why she can't go to bars or crowded restaurants anymore feels impossible. Her best friend from childhood tried to invite her to a family gathering last month, and María made an excuse. The thought of being in a room full of people, unable to control the environment, unable to leave quickly-it's paralyzing.

What troubles her most is how afraid she's become of her own reactions. She'll be working on something benign-animating a character's angry expression-and suddenly she's back in that kitchen, back in that moment of helplessness. Her hands shake. She closes the laptop. Sometimes she doesn't open it again for days.

She knows logically that James is gone, that she's safe. But her body hasn't caught up with that knowledge. Her nervous system has learned to see danger everywhere, and she doesn't know how to teach it otherwise.
